utterances.text: As far as I know, many Muslims expressed their wish to leave the town voluntarily. Everybody could leave. Serbs, Muslims alike. In my opinion, based on my conversations, I don't know whether they decided to go. The only thing I know is they wanted to be reunited with their families. It was a war. Some people had to move. They wanted to join them. They simply expressed their desire to be reunited with their family because many -- families because many of the people were fighting on the other side, and then when they left, nobody knew what the outcome of the battle would be. We won in the end, the Serbs won, but many of their units fled into the area controlled by the Muslim fighters. Some of them stayed. I know that they expressed their desire to leave. I know that buses were made ready. I was sitting there with a -- some friends of mine, Muslims. I know that many of them survived, thank God, and they said that they wanted to go because they wanted to join their families. They were all over the place. There was a war going on. It was chaos. I know that transportation was made ready for them. I know that because I was there. Nobody forced them to go. Serbs could go too. Muslims. Whoever. We did not mistreat them. We treated them nicely. We even provided them with an escort as they left. We did not force them to go. I swear before God the Serb and Muslim children played together. Some of our lads were killed and perhaps in fear of revenge -- because many of our soldiers, many of our lads, had been killed, but nobody, as far as I know, there was this group of individuals who were convicted, and if I had any knowledge, I would share it with you, I would say it now in court, and it's not all the soldiers in the VRS, all the officers, who should be tarred with this brush.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Traldi, I'm looking at the clock. We are one hour since we restarted.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: I think it's a good time for the break, Mr. President. I'll be under my estimate, so I'll be just 10 or 15 minutes when we resume.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, we will take a break of 20 minutes. And we would like see you back after that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We resume at quarter past 12.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: While we are waiting for the witness to be brought in, Mr. Ivetic, just in order to assist you, I read to you the guidance the Chamber gave on the 29th of October 2012. "However, the Chamber clarifies that a document's probative value may also be established by having a witness testify about events described in a certain document. If the content of a document used during a witness's examination is sufficiently linked to the content of that witness's testimony, the document may be appropriately tendered and admitted with that witness even if the witness is unfamiliar with the specific document." Now, the witness gave his testimony about that he couldn't believe that elderly would be detained in KP Dom, and I leave it alone whether the dates of birth of these witnesses are such that you could say it impeaches or does not impeach, but the link is sufficiently established with the testimony of the witness. That's what -- at least the guidance of the Chamber was at the time and still is.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And, Your Honours, where I have a problem is you asked if the same objection would apply to the document be it tendered under the bar table. Your Honours gave a guidance for the Prosecution to file their bar table submissions at the close of the Prosecution's --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: -- case in chief. To reopen the Prosecution's case in chief to allow documents to come in through the bar table during the Defence case is, I believe, contrary to that guidance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, I'm going to interrupt you. It is tendering a document. And if I say from the bar table, I meant to say that the witness may have no personal knowledge about the document, and that expression was often used when it came to tendering of a document where the witness couldn't say himself anything about it and that is not the same as being part of a bar table motion, a bar table motion which is then not directly linked to any specific portion of the evidence given by a witness. But if my -- the use of my words have confused you, then my apologies for it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Traldi.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Sir, I want to pick up where we were discussing immediately before the break. Now, you said both Muslims and Serbs were able to leave Foca. In fact, the people who did leave were overwhelmingly Muslims, right?

utterances.speaker: VESELINKO SIMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Now, the Chamber has received evidence that there were guards around Muslim houses in Foca town at that time, Serb guards. Were you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: VESELINKO SIMOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: The Chamber has already received evidence that women, children and elderly people from Muslim villages were brought into Foca and held in detention centres also with armed guards. Were you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I believe that misstates the evidence. If we can have a reference for it. I believe "detention centres" is the critical term.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Reception centres, Mr. Traldi.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: I think Mr. Ivetic has a specific witness's term in mind. I think different witnesses have used different terminology including during the Prosecution case, but I won't insist on the term. I'll rephrase if that suits the Chamber and Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: The Chamber has received evidence that women, children, and elderly people from Muslim villages were brought into Foca and held in buildings with armed guards around them. Were you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: VESELINKO SIMOVIC
utterances.text: Could you be more specific in your question? Where? What? I know about the guards that you were talking about. I know that we received orders to establish check-points in areas with Muslim majority, and there was a curfew at that check-point, after 8.00 no one was allowed to enter those parts of the town under arms. Maybe the -- that's the cause of confusion. I know about this check-point in the part of the town where I lived.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me stop you there. Listen carefully to the question. Women, children and elderly people brought into Foca and held in buildings. A check-point is not a building. A building with armed guards around them. And that's also not curfew. A building. Could you please answer whether you were aware of that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Based on what I know, I can say that some inhabitants demanded from the command and from the military police -- since this will be a lengthy explanation and I do apologise for that. The territory of the municipality of Foca is one of the largest municipalities, in terms of its surface area.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me stop you there. If you would please first answer the question. If there is any further explanation needed, then Mr. Traldi will ask for it. Again, were you aware of the persons I referred to being brought to Foca and being held in buildings with armed guards?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please, Mr. Traldi, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: The Chamber has also received evidence that crimes were committed against the people in those buildings. I take it you weren't aware of that either?

utterances.speaker: VESELINKO SIMOVIC
utterances.text: The only thing I do know is that Muslim residents -- well, the military police, I really cannot explain this briefly. If you want to hear my answer and if you want to get an accurate answer, I cannot give you a "yes" or "no" answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: A simple: Are you aware of any crimes committed against people in those buildings? And at this moment, if you say, "Well, I was not aware of any such crimes being committed in those buildings," then at the end of your testimony, if there is anything you'd like to add, you will have an opportunity to do so. Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, the problem comes in in that what are those buildings when the witness's answer --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: -- previously was not knowing about what buildings are being talked about. That's at line 10.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: As a matter of fact, he doesn't know that people were even held in buildings. To that extent, Mr. Traldi, it may --

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: That's why I included the words "I take it you weren't aware of that" in my question, Mr. President, and I expected the answer to be very brief.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. If you don't know about the persons, the elderly, children, being kept in buildings being guarded, then Mr. Traldi assumed that you would not know about any crimes committed under such circumstances. Was he right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Traldi.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Now, I put to you that all of those things could explain, could make someone feel, they had to leave, couldn't they? Certainly having armed guards around your house, that could make someone feel they had to leave, couldn't it?

utterances.speaker: VESELINKO SIMOVIC
utterances.text: I never saw any armed guards around any of the buildings. Based on your question, I can conclude that there were some buildings, but if you say that armed guards were stationed around houses, armed soldiers, I just don't understand it, so was it a building or was it a house? Based on what you said, it would seem that there were guards in front of all of the Muslim houses. That's the way I understand your question, that that's what your implying, that there were armed guards in front of the houses, Muslim houses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Traldi, you're asking first for an opinion, second on what, for the witness, is a hypothetical situation. That might not greatly assist the Chamber. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Let me put it this way, then: You don't know why, really, any of the Muslims who you say requested to leave Foca, you don't know why they made such a request, do you?

utterances.speaker: VESELINKO SIMOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And they had to make such a request, and had to leave in the buses you said were provided, with the escort you said was provided, because there were check-points on the roads like you described, right?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Objection, calls for speculation and does not follow from the evidence of the witness. If the witness says he doesn't know then to make this statement is really just presenting arguments.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, that's not, as a matter of fact -- Mr. Traldi, perhaps at -- may I take it that that such a request had to be made, that that is to some extent based on the evidence the Chamber heard before, and that you put all this to the witness. Could you phrase it in such a way that that's clear to everyone?

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: I think "had" perhaps may have been the problem and I should have phrased that a little bit differently, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Give it a try.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Sir, it was only possible to leave in the buses you said were provided to the Muslims with the escort you said was provided to the Muslims because, as you said, there were military check-points on the roads. That's right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: VESELINKO SIMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, but they left under escort because many of us, and our superiors, definitely, were concerned about the things that might happen to them because many of our lads had been killed and someone may have wanted to exact revenge, firing a round from the woods on the bus. And that's why --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, again, whether they may have good reasons or not, the question was whether it was only possible to leave in those buses, that you couldn't leave in another way.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, if they wanted to, they could leave any which way they wanted, but there were no cars, there was no fuel, it was -- there was a war going on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So you could leave not using the transportation provided, transportation by bus?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. But --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's an answer. Please, Mr. Traldi. If Mr. Traldi has any follow-up questions, he'll put them to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: I have two. First earlier this page you testified, I just want to make sure I understand it, that when these Muslims left in the buses, you believed that they might be in danger, those buses might be shot at, even as they were leaving the municipality, and that's why an escort was provided, right?

utterances.speaker: VESELINKO SIMOVIC
utterances.text: No. I did not say that. Some people wanted to go to Pljevlja. It's 75 kilometres through the woods from Foca to Pljevlja, and we were concerned. It was our fear that as they travelled through the woods, somebody that we could not see could do something that we didn't want to happen. They could have shot at the buses and do somethings that we did not want to happen. That's why they had military escort. In order to be able to travel safely. Because God forbid that something should happen. Many of our lads had been killed, as I said, and somebody could have -- from the woods, and if they had escort our soldiers would do something, they would capture this person, and that person would be held responsible. This is why they were under escort. Not because we didn't love them. Some people left on the buses and they were able to come back, and I am able to sit down and have a cup of coffee with them. I'm happy to see that they made it through.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Sir, I think you may have misunderstood my question. I think you've answered it in the end, but I hadn't asked about whether you loved the Muslims or who you had coffee with after the war. Simply for you to confirm, as you did, the reasons that a military escort was provided. So the second follow-up question I had was it wasn't, in fact, possible to leave in other ways, right? You said they could leave any way they wanted but not in cars, there was no gas, there were no cars. This was the way out, right?

utterances.speaker: VESELINKO SIMOVIC
utterances.text: Well, for Muslims who wanted to leave the town, that's what they thought. And I share that opinion right now. If you leave on foot, you could pass through the check-points, the fighters would let you through, but you could always come across some crazy guys, but they knew that if they had the escort of those proper fighters, they knew that they would be safe. And if you head out of the town where the Serb forces was stationed, well, you can come across a maniac who would shoot you just because you were a Muslim, and that's why they had escort on the route to Pljevlja, in order to avoid those consequences that we really did not want to see, women, children, honest people who just wanted to be reunited with their families on the opposite side. We didn't want them to be shot by somebody firing from the woods. This is something that we didn't want to happen.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And after those people had left, Foca was renamed Srbinje, right?

utterances.speaker: VESELINKO SIMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And calling it Srbinje of course labels it a Serb place, right?

utterances.speaker: VESELINKO SIMOVIC
utterances.text: No. Not really, sir. How should I explain it? Some poets invented that. You have Trebinje, Ljubina, Nevesinje, these are all towns in Herzegovina and that's why some poet came up with this idea that Srbinje sounds better than Foca. Every time people ask me where I'm from, I always say I'm from Foca. So Srbinje, Ljubina, Nevesinje, Trebinje. It's just a poetry, just to have a rhyme. Foca was called Foca for centuries and nothing has changed. Nothing has improved in our town after it was remained Srbinje. For me, it's Foca. It's just those poetic souls who came up with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: One of those poetic souls was the president of the Crisis Staff, Mr. Stanic, right?

utterances.speaker: VESELINKO SIMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And the Chamber has seen evidence that Momcilo Krajisnik, the president of the assembly, also started referring to Foca as Srbinje. Was he a poetic soul?

utterances.speaker: VESELINKO SIMOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I don't know Momcilo Krajisnik. He was a politician. Well, I just don't know. I don't know whether he was a poetic soul or not. But for Stanic, I do. For him, a sparrow was more important and stronger than any hawk.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Your Honours, that is completes my examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Traldi. Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I have a few questions, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sir, you were asked at temporary transcript page 27 if 50.000 Sandzaklije, fierce Sandzaklije came, and you said no. But did some Sandzaklije come to Foca; that is, people claiming to be Sandzaklije?

utterances.speaker: VESELINKO SIMOVIC
utterances.text: I did not see any Sandzakli men in Foca. I know that they attended the rally, the SDA rally in Foca. During the war, while the fighting was going on, I did not come across any Sandzakli men. I did come across many of their radical movements. They may have included Sandzakli people.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, you were asked about Zaga being convicted. Did Zaga and his unit get the same instruction on laws of war and treatment of civilians that your unit did, which you testified about today?

utterances.speaker: VESELINKO SIMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Every combatant, I claim that with full responsibility, could have read the order. It was hanging there at every command. A thousand times they could have read it. I've said this already and I'm telling you yet again: The court has sentenced you and it was too mild a sentence, and I don't need to repeat what I said. How I would have dealt with him. But may I say, none of the members of the Army of Republika Srpska, once they got under this command, they never received orders from their superior officers or commanders or generals to do that kind of thing. I mean really I shouldn't be repeating this time and again, but had I been his judge, he would have been killed by an electric chair and I would have pressed the button three times.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, sir, you said every combatant could have read the order. It was hanging there at every command. Whose order was hanging at every command?

utterances.speaker: VESELINKO SIMOVIC
utterances.text: The signature was general of the Army of Republika Srpska. The officer who would be reading this in front of a lineup of soldiers would have said this is what was ordered by the general of the Army of Republika Srpska, Ratko Mladic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And I'd like to call up P6685.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sir, you were shown this document by the Prosecution and you were asked if these men all appeared to be over the age of 50 years. The first question I have for you: Were there soldiers in the VRS in Foca that were over the age of 50 years?

utterances.speaker: VESELINKO SIMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I am just going to say one thing to answer this question to the public prosecutor: May God spare each and every country of any war. Sir, if somebody wants to carry a rifle, he can do that at the age of 80, too. My first commander Dragan Nikolic was killed bay soldier who was 73 years old. He fired at him. He walked into a house, he saw this old man, and this old man shot him. The young man who wanted to get him out was also killed by this 73 year old man. You did not -- well, I mean, I did not want to interrupt the Presiding Judge. Even a woman of 80 can carry a rifle if she wants to. So I was not allowed to explain that, that anyone could have carried a rifle. Dragan Nikolic, I state this publicly, he was killed by a soldier who was 73 years old.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And when you captured enemy prisoners of war in combat, did you know the ages of the fighters at that time?

utterances.speaker: VESELINKO SIMOVIC
utterances.text: It's not for me to question witnesses and to put questions to witnesses. That is done by other formations. I am supposed to act in accordance with the orders of my superiors. You know, in war, when you take someone prisoner, well, that is something that causes great fear, and I always treat these people fairly. I say that nobody is going to touch him once he gets -- once I bring him to the police. Well, then it is the police who take them over. Now, our command decides whether they will be taken to a prison or somewhere else. Most probably into this institution where POWs were being put up.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, according to your understanding of the Yugoslav All People's Defence, what were the ages for call-up of citizens for military duty? What were the age ranges?

utterances.speaker: VESELINKO SIMOVIC
utterances.text: Well, according to military formation, since did I my military service in the old Yugoslav army, it was from 18 to 50 that they could be called up. I'm not sure. 18 to 50, reserve duty in the army of Yugoslavia. I mean, I'm talking about this old system that I knew. I mean this new one, I never got to know it any way. So from the age of 18, sorry. 18 to 50, yes. People of that age could be called up.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, you mentioned check-points. What was the -- of -- what was the purpose of check-points? Was it to keep people out or to keep people in?

utterances.speaker: VESELINKO SIMOVIC
utterances.text: Well, no. Check-points were there because there were some Muslim settlements and then these criminals would go there, these criminals from Belgrade, most of them were criminals, and they tried to get in in order to gain some kind of benefit. Then the Crisis Staff in Foca decided to set up these check-points, and then after 7.30 no one was allowed to pass by these check-points. During the day we could act rapidly, but then at night-time -- well, once one of these criminals from Belgrade tried to pass by there and the young men wouldn't let him, and then he wanted to pass by nevertheless and then they killed him. He got killed because he wanted to pass by the check-point.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And when you say one of these criminals from Belgrade, whom are you talking about, what entity or formation did that individual belong to?

utterances.speaker: VESELINKO SIMOVIC
utterances.text: Well, this was the units that I talked about a moment ago. They have no unit. They were dogs of war. Dogs as we called them. They did not have a unit. They did not have any ideals. They had nothing. They just wanted to earn German marks in that way. They weren't interested in anything else.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, you were asked about crimes at buildings in Foca against Muslims. What was the procedure of your unit of military police for responding to complaints by Muslims of mistreatment in Foca?

utterances.speaker: VESELINKO SIMOVIC
utterances.text: Well, the task of our unit was to appear on the spot if anyone reported anything, to see who it was that mistreated these citizens, when, at what time, where, and of course we would arrest such a person.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And during the course of the war, did your military police unit, the Dragan Nikolic Intervention Unit, respond to such complaints from Muslim residents of Foca?

utterances.speaker: VESELINKO SIMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sir, again on behalf of my client and the rest of the team I thank you for your testimony.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honours I have no further questions in redirect.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Traldi, any need for further questions?

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Just very briefly arising out of the redirect, Mr. President. Further cross-examination by Mr. Traldi:

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sir, at temporary transcript page 59, you were recorded to say that Dragan Nikolic was your commander. Were you recorded correctly?

utterances.speaker: VESELINKO SIMOVIC
utterances.text: Dragan Nikolic was the commander, the first commander of the military police in the Territorial Defence. He wasn't my commander because he got killed. But I was trying to say, well, maybe I misspoke. Maybe I misspoke. My --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: That answers my question, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And that's all I had.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Traldi. Mr. Simovic, this concludes your testimony. I'd like to thank you very much for coming to The Hague and for having answered all the questions that were put to you by the parties and by the Bench, and I wish you a safe return home again. You may follow the usher.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But before I do so, there is only one thing. In response to one of the questions of Mr. Ivetic, you said, well, this was exactly the thing I wanted to explain. Earlier I had given you a promise that I would give you an opportunity to add whatever you'd like to add if it's related to the questions. Now, has that been covered by your answer to Mr. Ivetic's question or is there anything else you think you were unable to say while being stopped and therefore you'd like to tell us now?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. No. I just wanted to answer that question that was put by the gentleman, the public prosecutor. Well I've just answered so --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That's fine.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Again, we wish you a safe return home. Please follow the usher.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is the Defence ready to call its next witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: We are, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And that would be?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Nenad Deronjic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Could the witness be -- yes, Mr. Traldi?

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: With the witness having been excused, I'd just ask for the same courtesy, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, it's hereby given.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Next witness being Mr. Nenad Deronjic. No protective measures, scheduled for 30 minutes in chief and --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: We had sent an e-mail saying it was closer to 50 minutes with three additional documents, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Does that change in any way the assessment or the -- the two hours and 30 minutes the Prosecution has asked for?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Not really, Mr. President. In fact, I hope in studying all the material to be quite a bit less than that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's appreciated. Let's wait until the witness comes in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Deronjic. Before you give evidence, the rules require that you make a solemn declaration. May I invite to you make that solemn declaration of which the text is now handed out to you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Deronjic. Please be seated. Mr. Deronjic, you'll first be examined by Mr. Ivetic. You'll find had him to your left. Mr. Ivetic is a member of the Defence team for Mr. Mladic. Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Good day, sir.

utterances.speaker: NENAD DERONJIC
utterances.text: Good day.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I would like to start by calling up 1D0168 in e-court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, is it perhaps 1638?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: 1638, yes. I apologise if I misspoke.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sir, do you recognise the signature on the first page of the Serbian original of this statement?

utterances.speaker: NENAD DERONJIC
utterances.text: Yes. That is my signature on this statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And if we can turn to the last page of the document in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And again, sir, the question I pose: What can you tell us about the signature on this page of the document? Whose is it?

utterances.speaker: NENAD DERONJIC
utterances.text: I also confirm that this signature on the last page is my page [as interpreted], and this is the date that I wrote there.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, subsequent to signing this statement, did you have occasion to review the same and read it in the Serbian language so as to check its accuracy?

utterances.speaker: NENAD DERONJIC
utterances.text: This statement -- well, I didn't read it immediately after signing it. However, before I came here to The Hague, I read it in detail and I established certain things; namely, where there should be additional clarifications and additions in general.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Now I'd like to look at page 2 in both languages and paragraph 3 with you. And now that we have that on the screen, I'd like to ask you, sir, do you have any corrections or clarifications that you'd like to make to paragraph 3?

utterances.speaker: NENAD DERONJIC
utterances.text: Yes. In paragraph 3, I have a few clarifications. So may I clarify that?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yes, please go ahead, sir.

utterances.speaker: NENAD DERONJIC
utterances.text: This is it. In paragraph 3, it says that before the conflict broke out in Srebrenica in 1992, I was transferred to the Bratunac police station where I also worked as a policeman during the war up until 1996. However, from the 21st of July 1995, until 1996, I worked at the police station of Srebrenica. So this was not included here, and that is correct, for sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And as a follow-up question, is there any UN certification process that police had to go through after the conclusion of the war?

utterances.speaker: NENAD DERONJIC
utterances.text: Yes. All police officials, all active duty policemen who worked in the MUP of Republika Srpska after the war had to go through certain checks of the international police, that is to say the IPTF.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And were you certified under that process?

utterances.speaker: NENAD DERONJIC
utterances.text: Yes. Of course. I was certified, and I have certain certificates certifying that.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now if you can look at paragraph 6 --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Which is on the same page in the English and is on the fourth page in the Serbian. And I just -- there we go. Third page I apologise. The third page in the Serbian.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Here at paragraph 11, you say -- when you say, "I do not know where they are located now but I know they were archived at the police station in Bratunac," what is it that you are referring to? If it helps -- I apologise. In paragraph 6 you're talking about check-points, about the check-point in Konjevic Polje. Do you have any corrections you wish to make as to this check-point in Konjevic Polje?

utterances.speaker: NENAD DERONJIC
utterances.text: As for paragraph 6, I have some corrections as follows. At the check-point in Konjevic Polje, it was not the 2nd Company of the Special Police unit of the Zvornik security services centre. Rather, this work was done by police officials of PS Bratunac because Konjevic Polje belonged territorially to the municipality of Bratunac so that would be it. So it was not the 2nd Company of the PJP but rather it was the police officials from Bratunac.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Excuse me, if I -- and I know Mr. Ivetic is aware of this problem, but if we can try to ask the witness, when referring to his unit, to keep the initials PJP because there's a translation issue that makes it very difficult to distinguish between other units, if we -- if we go into the full name of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: That's understood by myself and Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sir, when referring to your 2nd Company of the separate police unit or "posebna jedinica policije" of the Zvornik police station, could you please refer to them by the acronym PJP, or in B/C/S PJP?

utterances.speaker: NENAD DERONJIC
utterances.text: All right. I'll be using that expression, PJP.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, if we can look at page -- the next page in English and also in Serbian, and paragraph 11, which is on this page.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Here you say: "I do not know where they are located now, but I know that they were archived at the police station in Bratunac." What are you referring to in this paragraph?

utterances.speaker: NENAD DERONJIC
utterances.text: This paragraph has to do with patrol orders. These were reports that we wrote every day when we would complete our work and that we would bring to the police station in Bratunac. These were daily reports as to how many vehicles and persons were checked and whether there were any problems at that check-point on that day during that shift.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And if we can look at paragraph 20 on this page, which should not be broadcast, page 4 in the English and page 5 in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Can you please explain for us in more detail what you meant to say here about why the difference in dates for the document that is referenced not being unusual?

utterances.speaker: NENAD DERONJIC
utterances.text: As far as appointments are concerned, for police work, that is to say the work that I carried out at the public security station in Srebrenica, the appointment could have been on the basis of an order or a dispatch from the chief of the Public Security Services centre, whereas employment papers are something that I could get later on. That's what happens to this day. The order is important, that -- so that it could be carried out immediately, whereas the appointment follows later.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Now, apart from the clarifications and corrections that we have gone through now, do you stand by everything else that is written in your statement as being accurate?

utterances.speaker: NENAD DERONJIC
utterances.text: Yes. Except for these changes and clarifications. I accept the rest of the statement and it is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And if I were to ask you today questions based on these same topics as contained in your written statement, would your answers to those questions be the same in substance as to what is recorded in your statement?

utterances.speaker: NENAD DERONJIC
utterances.text: Yes. The answers would be the same in substance as those provided in this statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, you've taken the solemn declaration today to tell the truth. Would those answers as contained in your written statement be truthful?

utterances.speaker: NENAD DERONJIC
utterances.text: Yes. The answers are truthful.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I would tender 1D1638 under seal at this time due to I believe two paragraphs that I'm not sure whether the information contained therein relates to matters that were in private session with a protected witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 1D1638 receives number D584, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D584 is admitted under seal.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, may I put one question in relation to this statement to the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Sir, you were asked earlier if you had the occasion to review this statement and read it in the Serbian language. Then you said: "This statement -- well, I didn't read it immediately after signing it." I would like to know did you read it before signing it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. I signed that statement and later, because of some work obligations, I did not have time to read it, but just before I came to The Hague, I read it in detail and that's how I realised that some of these clarifications were needed in certain paragraphs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Is that not a quite unusual way to sign something without reading the text?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, yes. But I was busy at the time. I had these work obligations. I signed the statement. I didn't read it immediately. But I did subsequently. As I've already told you, before I left for The Hague, I read it in detail and realised that these clarifications were needed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Your Honours, at this time I would read a public summary of the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Just one second. Could I ask you -- Judge Fluegge may have a few more questions on this issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Just briefly, can you tell me where and under what circumstances you signed this statement?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I signed that statement in Bratunac. That is to say, during working hours while I was on duty. I signed it in a catering establishment in the presence of Nenad Petrusic who provided that statement to me. I didn't stay there for a very long time. It was very brief because I was really very busy. I had these work obligations. I didn't read it and signed it and that's that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: And Mr. Petrusic visited you there. Did he indicate that he will come?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I did not quite understand what you said. What do you mean by that, that he will come?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: He visited you at the police station, at the catering unit. Did you expect him to come? Was there -- did he call you before or how did that come about?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] He called me. He phoned me. When he arrived, he phoned me and he said that I should come to this cafe actually, that I should take that statement and sign it and that's that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: What cafe?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's a coffee bar, you know, Nap [phoen]. That's where we met. He said that he would be there. So I was working then. This was during working hours. I came there for five or ten minutes, signed that, and things followed as I've already explained to you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I've two follow-up questions in this respect. Did you ever see a draft of the statement or was it the first time at that moment, although not having time to read it, that you saw it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That was the first time, but I was interviewed on three occasions by him in my house. And based on those conversations, he put together this statement that he gave me to sign.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Did Mr. Petrusic accept that you had no time and that you would just sign or did he insist on you reading it before you would sign it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, he accepted that. He knew that I didn't have enough time. He didn't have enough time either, probably, and I was in a big hurry and that's how it was done.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And you had confidence that the statement which you had not read, that it would reflect the interviews that had taken place?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I trusted him, of course, because we had met on three occasions before that and we discussed this statement and everything related to it already.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you for those answers. Mr. Ivetic, I think I interrupted you when were you about to start reading the summary, but perhaps you better do that after the break.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We take a break, Witness, and we would like to see you back in 20 minutes from now. Would you please follow the usher.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We resume at 25 minutes to 2.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We are waiting for the witness to be brought into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Deronjic, we will first hear Mr. Ivetic reading a summary of your testimony. Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. The witness is a professional policeman who worked in the police station in Bratunac and later the police station in Srebrenica before transferring to the border police. He was also a member of the 2nd Company of the PJP from the Zvornik police station -- I'm told there is a problem with the translation, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Has it been fixed? Then please --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I'm told it's good.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: The witness is a professional policeman who worked in the police station in Bratunac and later the police station in Srebrenica before transferring to the border police. He was also a member of the 2nd Company of the PJP from the Zvornik police station as were others from the Bratunac police station. In early July 1995, the witness mostly worked as a member of the Bratunac police station at a check-point at Konjevic Polje at the intersection of the roads leading to Vlasenica and Zvornik. On 11 July 1995, the witness was discharging his duties at that location and left at 8.00 a.m., 12 July 1995, having finished his shift. Thereafter, he was activated as part of the 2nd Company of the PJP and told to be on stand-by due to the situation in Srebrenica. At 1500 hours, 12 July 1995, he and other members of that PJP company were sent to Srebrenica to patrol the town and protect property from looting, while the SJB Srebrenica was being set up. He stayed as part of the PJP in Srebrenica eight days. The witness was officially transferred to a full time -- as an employee of the newly set up SJB Srebrenica on 21 July 1995. The witness refutes the testimony of Momir Nikolic that he was present at the check-point at Konjevic Polje on 13 July 1995, given that he was discharging different duties as a member of the PJP in Srebrenica town during that time. And that completes the summary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you have any further questions for the witness, please proceed, Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sir, if we can look at paragraph 23 of your statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And it's the next page in both languages, and that page also should not be broadcast.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Here, in this paragraph 23, what do you mean when you say it was generally known that Momir Nikolic told a number of untruths about you and others?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could we have the English on the right-hand of the screen?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sir, could you answer the question and tell us what it is that you meant when you said it is generally known in Bratunac that in his testimony Momir Nikolic told a number of untruths concerning not only me but other people who lived in the Bratunac area?

utterances.speaker: NENAD DERONJIC
utterances.text: Well, as for Momir Nikolic, as I have already stated, it is general knowledge in Bratunac. Based on my contacts with some people in Bratunac, I can say that Momir Nikolic said a number of untruths or rather lies not only about me but about some other people who lived or live in the Bratunac area.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And do you know any specifics or is it just general knowledge?

utterances.speaker: NENAD DERONJIC
utterances.text: Well, I don't have any specifics. This is just some general information that I received based on my conversations with some people in Bratunac.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If the witness has no further specifics, Mr. Ivetic, I think we can move on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: If I may just ask one question, Mr. Ivetic, if you don't mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Do you know of any reason why Mr. Nikolic would tell lies about you and other people?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I really don't know. It is my opinion that he told lies about me and other people in order to get a more beneficial position for himself, to protect himself, and to acquit himself of some of the accusations against him and some of the things that he did.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I'd like to now ask --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I'm just wondering. You said you have no further specifics. You were talking about lies. Is this -- the one you responded to, is that the only one or is -- are there other lies about yourself?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, the lie that I know of specifically is the thing that he told about me being there while I wasn't there, but some people told me that he also lied about them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But there are no other lies about you that you could specify?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't have any other knowledge of any other lies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now I'd like to ask you some more questions. First, could you tell us about the PJP? Who are called up as members of the PJP?

utterances.speaker: NENAD DERONJIC
utterances.text: No. As regards the PJP of the secure -- public security service in Zvornik, all the police officers in the police stations at the level of the centre were there, which means that the Zvornik police station, or the police officers who did their regular police work there, were members of the platoons of the Special Police units, the PJP. So they were all involved in the six companies, two people from one station, four people from another station, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And was engagement in the PJP a full-time permanent engagement or was it temporary?

utterances.speaker: NENAD DERONJIC
utterances.text: It was for temporary and special tasks.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: When a policeman such as yourself was called up into the PJP in 1992 to 1995, did you continue to perform your regular duties at the police station in addition to your duties within the PJP?

utterances.speaker: NENAD DERONJIC
utterances.text: When we were engaged in the PJP, we were given special tasks from the Security Services Centre, which meant that we no longer did our regular work in police stations, the kind of work that we usually did as police officers.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Where would you receive your pay during the time that you were engaged as a PJP member performing PJP duties?

utterances.speaker: NENAD DERONJIC
utterances.text: I received my salary from the MUP of Republika Srpska, through the Bratunac police station for a while, and later on, when I moved to the police station in Srebrenica, I received my salary from the Srebrenica police station while I was in PJP.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Would you still report to the station commander during this time period when you were activated in the PJP, or to someone else?

utterances.speaker: NENAD DERONJIC
utterances.text: While we were engaged in the PJP, we did not submit any reports because we were accompanied by the company commanders. I'm talking about PJP companies.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And what was your experience, how long could a PJP activation or engagement last, how many days?

utterances.speaker: NENAD DERONJIC
utterances.text: Seven, ten to fifteen days. On occasion, we would be involved in combat for 15 days in the field.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And during the time period 1992 through 1995, what was the most frequent assignment that was the reason for one to be activated into the PJP?

utterances.speaker: NENAD DERONJIC
utterances.text: Most often the assignments given to the PJP members was to hold the lines, combat lines. We were at Treskavica, Bandijerka and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, you said earlier today that while working at the check-point at Konjevic Polje, you were fulfilling duties as a Bratunac police station policeman. Just to be clear, I want you to tell us at what time in July of 1995 were you called up or activated and engaged as a PJP policeman.

utterances.speaker: NENAD DERONJIC
utterances.text: I was activated on the 12th of July 1995, as a member of the PJP.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And when after the 12th of July 1995, did that activation or engagement in the PJP end?

utterances.speaker: NENAD DERONJIC
utterances.text: It ended with the activities in Srebrenica on the 20th of July 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: During the eight days that were you at Srebrenica as a member of the 2nd Company of the Zvornik PJP, where were you billeted to sleep?

utterances.speaker: NENAD DERONJIC
utterances.text: While we were in Srebrenica, performing those tasks, we were billeted in the Srebrenica police station, and for a while we slept in buildings referred as miner's buildings which are further up from the police station.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And where did you obtain your food during that time period, those eight days?

utterances.speaker: NENAD DERONJIC
utterances.text: Food would be delivered to us, or rather throughout the time when we were involved in PJP, we would have food provided to us.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: During that time period, those eight days in Srebrenica, was there any functioning mode of public transportation in Srebrenica town, where you were at?

utterances.speaker: NENAD DERONJIC
utterances.text: No. There was no public transport at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: What was the way that you would move about or transport from the police station to the duty post and back?

utterances.speaker: NENAD DERONJIC
utterances.text: We would go from the police station to our duty post on foot. I'm talking about the various sectors and check-points.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And where were you assigned for duty on the 12th and 13th of July 1995 in Srebrenica, for instance? What -- what part of town?

utterances.speaker: NENAD DERONJIC
utterances.text: On the 12th of July, I was in the 1st sector, which covers the town itself, from the hotel to the culture hall, the department store, the municipal building, and the police station itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Did you at any time leave Srebrenica town during the period of 12 to 20 July 1995?

utterances.speaker: NENAD DERONJIC
utterances.text: No. I never left Srebrenica in that period. In fact, I did not reach the check-point on the road to Bratunac, which is located at the football pitch.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, in paragraph 17 of your statement --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And this page should not be broadcast. It's page 4 in English, page 5 in Serbian, and I'll wait for that to come up.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: -- you say that your task was to try and protect property from various groups which came in there to loot the abandoned property. Who or what are you talking about, these groups?

utterances.speaker: NENAD DERONJIC
utterances.text: To be more specific, those were not groups. Those were individuals. You have inhabitants of Srebrenica, civilians, women, who went to their homes, and there were also some armed individuals.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. And now I'd like to turn to paragraph 11 of your statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Which should be on the prior page in both versions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: May I ask for a clarification of the last answer of the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Sir, in your statement, you are talking about various groups which came there in order to loot the abandoned property. Now you are talking about inhabitants of Srebrenica, civilians, women, who went to their homes. And there were also some armed individuals. I don't understand this answer. Can you clarify that, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I can explain. For instance, if somebody comes in to loot property, they would be driving a tractor and they never go alone because they have to load lots of stuff so you would have three or four people.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Your task was to protect property from various groups. Who referred to various groups? Your superiors who tasked you with protecting property? Or was it your assumption that these groups would appear?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, it probably came from our superiors, and it did transpire. This was the task that we were given when we arrived in Srebrenica but those were not organised group of any sort. This did not require us to perform any other activities or anything.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: What did you mean by "it did transpire"? Did such groups appear on the scene?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, there were no organised groups. What I'm trying to say is if you say a group, you can mean three or four people on a tractor coming in to loot, to take a couple of bigger things. So it's a group. You cannot take out a refrigerator or some other larger items from a house on your own.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, the word "group" or "various groups" appears in your statement. These are your words, if they are your words.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that's what I said, but this was the task that we were given. Those were our orders. And it said specifically "groups," but I'm telling you I did not see any groups. We received this order from our superiors, our task was to deal with those groups, and this is what I quoted, the order, in my statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: And you just a minute ago said, "And it did transpire." What transpired?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, as I've already said, I did not see any organised groups doing those things. There were civilians, they were residents of Srebrenica who had come back, and there were those people who would come in on small tractors, four or five of them. Now, I don't know if you can really refer to them as groups. But that's what happened.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Are you saying that the residents of Srebrenica who came back were looting private property?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, there were cases of them doing that because their apartments had been destroyed, their stuff had been taken, and then they had to enter other people's houses in order to do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I have one more question in this respect. Witness, you then did see armed men looting?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I did see them on some occasions, and there was a case that turned out to be a problem. I saw a man with some calves. He had a rifle.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You've answered my question. Now, what did you then do? Did you arrest him? Did you round them up? Did you give them to your superiors? What did you do?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well to be quite frank we did not arrest him. We did not do anything because we had a problem. He trained his rifle on us and he had chambered around. In order to avoid problems we just let him pass.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So you're there as armed police officers to protect the property of others, and then you say, well, they were using their arms so we didn't do anything? Is that really your testimony about the way in which you performed your task or did not perform your task?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, this was the only case. We simply wanted to avoid trouble. We didn't want to shoot to kill this person. We knew that that man had cattle before the war and we simply let him go. It was the only thing to do, really.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So it happened you saw -- during all those days you saw only one person involved in looting which you then decided not to arrest?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There were other cases too, but I can't really remember all that, but I'm sure there were other cases, where we would seize the property, the goods, and we would put it in special warehouses. Some of it was stored in the police station and some of it was stored in the department store where there was a warehouse where all those seized objects were stored.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Did you make a document in which you described what you had seized and was that given to your superior command so as to report on your activities?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. We did not produce any documents. We handed the items to whoever was on duty in the warehouse and then they made a list of all the items that were handed over.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And what did you do with those who had committed that looting? Did you arrest them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. We did not arrest them. We just seized the items.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: It may be helpful, especially since we are almost over, if we could get the ethnicity of the people who are coming back. It's all very potentially misleading.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sir, you've heard Mr. McCloskey's question. Are you able to provide any information as to the ethnicity of the people that were coming back to Srebrenica town during the time period you were patrolling there, those eight days?

utterances.speaker: NENAD DERONJIC
utterances.text: The persons coming back to Srebrenica, who were in Srebrenica at the time, were of Serb ethnicity.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, do you have more questions on that document?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No I have no further questions. No. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I'd like to look at paragraph 11 of your statement. You mention a duty logbook that deputy commander Nedeljkovic was in charge of. What station this a logbook of?

utterances.speaker: NENAD DERONJIC
utterances.text: This duty logbook or roster of personnel with the schedule was in the public security station in Bratunac.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: At this time I'd like to call up 65 ter number 31002.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, document is not in e-court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Then we will go with the Defence version of the same. One moment. Can we try it again, 31002?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sir, do you recognise the document that is on the screen, and if so, could you identify it for us?

utterances.speaker: NENAD DERONJIC
utterances.text: Yes. I do recognise this document. It is a list of personnel employed in the Bratunac police station, with the date. It's in the upper portion. We are talking about July 1995. This is where you entered the activities of police officers, the duty that they performed in that period, the tasks that they did.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, looking at the English, since that's the easier one to read, we see certain notations such as the acronyms "PR" and "BD". What is the different -- what is the meaning of these two and what is their difference?

utterances.speaker: NENAD DERONJIC
utterances.text: Those acronyms refer to these things. PR means on stand-by, and BD means that on that day, this police officer was doing combat duty.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And if we can go to the second page in the English, and it should still be the same page in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Entry number 36 on this document appears to relate to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And if we could scroll over to the column that is for the 10th, and the 11th of July and zoom-in on that in the B/C/S original perhaps.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sir, there is another acronym in Cyrillic for those two dates filled in for you. Could you please read into the record what is in Cyrillic for those two dates, the 10th and the 11th of July 1995?

utterances.speaker: NENAD DERONJIC
utterances.text: 10th and 11th of July, KP, from 8 to 8, that's the 10th, and the 11th it says, again, from 8 to 8, KP. Konjevic Polje.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And is that what -- what does the KP stand for, just so we are clear.

utterances.speaker: NENAD DERONJIC
utterances.text: KP stands for Konjevic Polje, the check-point at Konjevic Polje.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: And below the time frame, from 8 to 8, there is something else written. Can you explain what that is?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Perhaps try to zoom in on those two boxes maybe.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, it's not very legible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Can you see that now, entry 36?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, this is probably the time spent at check-point 24. I assume that it means 24 hours. That's what it seems to me. I think that's 24.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And if we look --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. President, just to confirm that is our own reading of this document as well. And I know the English translation has question marks, but our people that are good at this agree with that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It would then read, KP 08-08, underlined, and then is that what you're referring to?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Yes, 24, 24, and below that, 24.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. And is it then the understanding that it would be both times, 08-08, 24, or is it the second time any different? I do not know, Mr. Ivetic, whether you have any interpretation of what we see here.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I think that's what it appears to say. The English of course does not have that, which is why I was going through these entries, and this was -- the B/C/S came from the Prosecution. That's why we had a Defence version. The version used in Karadzic did not have the B/C/S original, and Mr. McCloskey was kind enough to provide that for us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So therefore both parties understand it to be 08, 08 underlined and then 24.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: With a KP in Cyrillic above it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, with KP in Cyrillic above it. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Your Honours, I see we are past the point for today. Should we --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: -- stop?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You're right. Mr. Ivetic, may I take it that you need tomorrow another 15 to 20 minutes? Is that --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Approximately 15, closer to 15.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Mr. Deronjic, we will adjourn for the day. utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.
